title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts): complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. We explicitly state that two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation semantics and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. We present the artifact‑grounded execution and analysis, diagnose why the design produced a null outcome, report representative task difficulty diagnostics, and give concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs are now widely proposed for intent→configuration tasks in NetOps because they can translate operator instructions into device configurations and procedural staged changes (canaries, progressive rollouts, rollback). Prior work shows LLMs produce syntactically plausible configurations but also cautions that operational safety depends on end‑to‑end behavior that includes generation variability, deterministic verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, rollback, and provenance. To probe whether a deterministic runtime verifier meaningfully changes end‑to‑end safety outcomes we preregistered a paired confirmatory study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) executed on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1.

Research question. Under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline); the experimental design and analysis plan were frozen prior to execution.

Key contribution and high‑level finding. We deliver (1) a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with all execution and analysis artifacts archived; (2) a clear, artifact‑grounded diagnosis showing that preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics plus reuse of a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling effect (universal acceptance) making the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction; and (3) concrete, implementable benchmark‑hardening recommendations grounded in the archived traces and execution accounting.
sections.related_work:
Intent‑to‑configuration pipelines, IaC automation, and verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair architectures form the primary technological antecedents for this study. Recent intent‑based configuration demonstrations and pretraining/fine‑tuning studies (e.g., intent‑based translation, PreConfig, GraphSynth) validate that LLMs can synthesize usable configuration templates in controlled benchmarks. In IaC contexts, verifier‑guided loops (e.g., TerraFormer) show measurable correctness gains in provisioning tasks; these motivate similar integrations in NetOps but leave open how runtime verifiers alter live staged‑rollout safety.

Deterministic verifiers and reachability tools (header‑space and related approaches) are effective at detecting configuration errors in offline and emulated settings but differ in scope and modelling assumptions (overlay vs. underlay, Kubernetes vs. IP networks). Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) increase functionality for AIOps/RCA tasks but introduce new failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tools, and miscalibrated confidence—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployment. Surveys highlight an evaluation gap: community‑standard action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited. Our experiment operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to directly probe verifier utility under those constraints.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory estimand. The study preregistration (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) fixed a paired binary confirmatory design with exactly N=400 tasks and the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline estimand. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 implemented the preregistered permutation‑based paired difference test (two‑sided, α=0.05) and an exact McNemar two‑sided test as a corroborating statistic. Bootstrap percentile CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary summaries.

Adapter semantics, shared generation, and model‑call accounting. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Crucially, the preregistered adapter semantics set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): one deterministic LLM generation was requested per task and that identical candidate was delivered to both the baseline and guarded episodes. This isolation targeted measurement of validator acceptance behavior on identical generator outputs rather than exposing independent generator variance between conditions. Model call accounting reflects this design: planned episodes = 800 (two episodes per task) while model_calls_used = 400 (one shared LLM call per task). The preregistration recorded this mapping and the execution manifest confirms it.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter: (a) requested a shared initial candidate from gpt‑5‑mini; (b) delivered it to both baseline and guarded episodes; (c) in the guarded episode deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full intent‑constraint validation and, per the preregistered repair policy, could invoke up to one repair attempt. The runtime guard implementation recorded validator_trace entries that include repair_applied flags, normalized_configuration, validation_before/after states, difficulty metadata, and the final validity decision. In practice, repair_applied = false for all episodes in this run.

Deterministic replay and exclusion rules. The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks: each agent+simulator pair was replayed three times and tasks with non‑identical replay outcomes or simulator errors were to be flagged and excluded from the primary analysis. The missingness plan mandated deterministic, automated exclusion without human adjudication. In this execution all deterministic consistency checks passed; no exclusions were applied.

Task generation and difficulty labeling. Tasks were generated deterministically with deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and include structured difficulty metadata (fields: changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, and level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). Representative example entries in the archived manifest show medium, hard, and very_hard patterns (representative sample: 1 medium, 2 hard, 3 very_hard among the first six tasks). The full per‑task difficulty labels for N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; the manifest was recorded verbatim during execution.

Diagnostic interpretation. The universal acceptance by the deterministic validator under shared candidates is the proximate cause of the observed ceiling and the null paired effect: when generator outputs are identical and a deterministic verifier consistently accepts that output, both conditions necessarily produce identical safe‑deploy outcomes.
sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two preregistered design choices combined to produce the deterministic ceiling: (A) shared_initial_generation delivered identical generator outputs to both baseline and guarded episodes, intentionally isolating validator acceptance on identical strings; and (B) the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). These choices remove independent generator variance and conflate acceptance and scoring, yielding identical decisions across paired episodes when the validator deterministically accepts the shared candidate.

Consequences for power and interpretation. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and intra‑pair variability such that an absolute difference of ≈0.10 would be detectable with N=400; the observed ceiling invalidates these assumptions and collapses uncertainty. The permutation and McNemar tests correctly reflect the identical outcomes (p = 1.0) but do not support inference about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. Therefore the null result should not be interpreted as evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary in general—rather, it is a direct artifact of the frozen design choices and implementation homogeneity.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden action‑aware benchmarks. Based on archived traces and the preregistered plan we recommend the following implementable steps for future confirmatory runs:

1) Independent per‑condition generation: set independent_condition_generation = true so each condition receives an independently sampled generator output, enabling generator variance to expose guard interventions.

2) Separate runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: use distinct verifier implementations (or independent scorers) to avoid conflating acceptance and scoring and to enable true adjudication of disagreements.

3) Controlled adversarial seeding: preregister a controlled fraction of perturbation/adversarial seeds to guarantee a measurable baseline failure rate and thereby preserve power for confirmatory detection.

4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling or oversampling: ensure an adequate representation of very_hard patterns so the benchmark contains non‑negligible error rates for statistical detection.

5) Repair accounting and instrumented rollback metrics: enable and record repair invocations, attempted repairs, and rollback times as preregistered secondary outcomes to measure operational mitigation efficacy.

These recommendations are grounded in the archived validator_trace structure (which supplies repair_applied, validation_before/after, and difficulty metadata) and in the execution accounting that revealed shared_initial_generation semantics and model call counts.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Model and scope: the run used a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator; results do not generalize across models, verifier implementations, or production heterogeneity. Environment realism: the benchmark is synthetic and the simulator/validator do not capture production telemetry noise or adversarial actor behaviors. Construct validity: reusing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer conflates acceptance and scoring. Adversarial robustness and human‑in‑the‑loop efficacy were not exercised and remain open.

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners considering verifier integration, our artifact‑grounded diagnosis demonstrates two practical lessons: (i) design choices that remove generation variance can hide the effectivity of runtime guards; (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human reviewers) are important for measuring guard impact. Benchmarks intended to validate runtime safety mechanisms should (and can, per our recommendations) be carved to maintain signal for guard interventions.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic runtime validator and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from preregistered design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. Our artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations offer concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; the manuscript reports representative sample counts (first six tasks) to illustrate benchmark diversity but does not fabricate the aggregated N=400 counts.
